Inverted parabola as a stable steady solution of the Surface Growth Model

Won-Suk Lee Address: Department of Physics & Astronomy, Seoul National University, 1 Gwanak-ro, Gwanak-gu, Seoul, 08826, Republic of Korea Email address: lookatme@snu.ac.kr
Abstract.

For the surface growth model under molecular beam epitaxy on ℝ\mathbb{R}, we show that an inverted parabola is a stable steady solution in the sense that any small perturbation of it decays in L∞​(ℝ)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) at the rate O(t−1/2logt)O(t^{-1/2}\log t). The proof is based on the explicit solution operator generated by the linearized perturbation equation. This result partially justifies the merging of two neighboring islands into a bigger one. Moreover, any derivative of its solution is shown to be decaying in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) for sufficiently small initial data.

Key words and phrases: 
surface growth model, steady solution, asymptotic stability, linearized perturbation, decay estimate, bootstrap argument
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
35B35, 35B40, 35C15, 35K55, 82C24

1. Introduction

In this paper we consider the initial value problem of molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) in surface growth model (SGM). Though it is motivated by the 2-dimensional physics, we consider the 1-dimensional problem

(1.1) {ut+ux​x​x​x+ux​x=−(ux2)x​x,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),\begin{split}\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}u_{t}+u_{xxxx}+u_{xx}&=-(u_{x}^{2})_{xx},\\ u(0,x)&=u_{0}(x),\end{array}\right.\end{split}

where x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, t≥0t\geq 0. This equation is to be solved for the time-dependent surface height u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) from the reference level. It is based on the continuity equation where the time derivative term is in general proportional to the Laplacian of the chemical potential terms and that explains why every term with spatial derivatives includes second derivatives. The second derivative term ux​xu_{xx} reflecting the linear instability is sometimes omitted, but in this paper we include this term into the analysis. The nonlinear term −(ux2)x​x-(u_{x}^{2})_{xx} is often called conserved KPZ term which is introduced by Villain [15] and contributes to the breaking of up-down symmetry of the system. It is related to the phenomena observed in the numerical simulation [13] (and also in experimental results [8]).

In recent decades, several mathematicians have studied stability using a Lyapunov functional (e.g. [3]) or in the sense of statistics (e.g. [1]), as well as well-posedness and regularity (e.g. [3], [4], [7], [11] and [13]) . Also, it has been known that there is a quadratic steady solution u⁡(t,x)=a−(1/4)​(x−b)2u(t,x)=a-(1/4)(x-b)^{2}(e.g. [12]). Numerical results point out that the solution smoothly grows except for the points of local minima which are considered to be the candidates for singularities (for details, see [13]). However, finite-time singularity formation from general initial data is still an open problem for (1.1).

There are three types of steady solutions and among them the inverted parabolae often appear in numerical simulations mentioned above. While the details are described in the appendix (summarized in Theorem A.1), it is supported by the physics in the background of the surface growth model. The stationarity is obtained by balancing diffusion and uphill currents that stop particles from spreading out. Chemical potential makes particles prefer places with lower curvature. Consequently it becomes unfavorable to form a steep hill. Meanwhile, there also exist uphill currents — e.g. one due to Schwoebel barrier — that prevent the collapse of hills. It can be compared to a sand grain failing to slip down from the slope due to friction. In such natural situations where there are competing opposite forces and the system has a preferred direction, a concave curve often turns out to be an equilibrium and even stable.

As the initial data u0​(x)u_{0}(x) evolves to u⁡(t,x)u(t,x), we define the perturbation v⁡(t,x)=u⁡(t,x)−[(1/2)−(1/4)​x2]v(t,x)=u(t,x)-[(1/2)-(1/4)x^{2}], whose behavior is governed by (1.2). Our goal is to prove the asymptotic stability of v⁡(t,x)=0v(t,x)=0 (corresponding to the steady solution itself) and to determine the rate at which it converges to zero. Here v0v_{0} represents an initial perturbation from the quadratic steady part, so we have to impose restrictions on the scale of v0v_{0}. That condition is stated in Theorem 1.1.

(1.2) vt+vx​x​x​x−(xvx​x)x=−∂x2(vx2).v_{t}+v_{xxxx}-(xv_{xx})_{x}=-\partial_{x}^{2}(v_{x}^{2}).
Theorem 1.1.

Let the initial data v0v_{0} be in (L1∩H5)​(ℝ)(L^{1}\cap H^{5})(\mathbb{R}). Then there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that the condition ‖v0‖H5​(ℝ)≤ϵ||v_{0}||_{H^{5}(\mathbb{R})}\leq\epsilon is sufficient for the existence and uniqueness of a classical global-in-time solution v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) of (1.2) converging to zero in L∞​(ℝ)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}). If v0∈Hσ​(ℝ)v_{0}\in H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{R}) with an integer σ>5\sigma>5, then this regularity persists. Also, ||v(t,⋅)||L∞​(ℝ)=O(t−1/2logt)||v(t,\cdot)||_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})}=O(t^{-1/2}\log t).

v0v_{0} being small is decided by the following conditions:

  • •

    γ⁡(ϵ0)<1\gamma(\epsilon_{0})<1, where γ\gamma is defined in Theorem 4.1 of Section 4.

  • •

    For some real number ρ>1/2\rho>1/2, it is satisfied that

    (1.3) ‖v0‖L2​(ℝ)≤min1≤n≤5⁡{1Cn​2​ρ−1ρ2​(ρ+1)​(2​n−1)},||v_{0}||_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}\leq\min_{1\leq n\leq 5}\left\{\frac{1}{C_{n}}\sqrt{\frac{2\rho-1}{\rho^{2}(\rho+1)}(2n-1)}\right\},

    where CnC_{n} is a sequence of constant numbers for Moser-type estimate in (3.4).

Remark 1.2.

Requirement of L1L^{1} is in accordance with the finite mass deviation from the steady solution (1/2)−(1/4)​x2(1/2)-(1/4)x^{2}, though it does not exactly match due to the issue of sign. This interpretation can be extended to the 2-dimensional problem, from which the problem is motivated.

Remark 1.3.

In short, small deviation from the parabola disappears. If a curve with two hills whose maximal points are sufficiently close — e.g. a small narrow Gaussian perturbation — then they will merge into a single bigger hill. Figure 1 visualizes the decay of v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) with the Gaussian initial data. Though it is not about the detailed mechanism, this supports the plausibility of the coarsening process generally known in material science. For more details, see [8].

The remaining sections are organized as follows: Before considering (1.2), we ignore the nonlinear term and analyze the linearized equation in Section 2. Some stability properties and additional regularities given by the solution-generating semigroup related to (2.1) will also be discussed. In Section 3 we get back to the equation including the nonlinear term and try to obtain some a priori energy estimates in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). Based on those results, we prove the stability of (1.2) in the sense of Theorem 1.1 in Section 4. The well-posedness of (1.2) is discussed in Section 5, to support the validity of all the preceding statements.

2. Linearized Perturbation of SGM

Before considering the full equation for v⁡(t,x)v(t,x), we linearize the equation around v=0v=0,

(2.1) wt+wx​x​x​x−(x​wx​x)x=0.w_{t}+w_{xxxx}-(xw_{xx})_{x}=0.

As this solution can be explicitly solved, we can construct many useful statements directly from the formula. In addition to the following proposition, in Section 2.3 we investigate L2L^{2} estimates related to (2.1).

Proposition 2.1.

If the initial data w0∈(L1∩H1)​(ℝ)w_{0}\in(L^{1}\cap H^{1})(\mathbb{R}) is given, then there is a solution w⁡(t,x)w(t,x) to (2.1) whose explicit form is expressed in (2.10). Moreover, for any nonnegative integer nn, ‖∂xnw⁡(t,⋅)‖L∞​(ℝ)||\partial_{x}^{n}w(t,\cdot)||_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})} satisfies the decay O(t−(n+1)/2logt)O(t^{-(n+1)/2}\log t) as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty.

Throughout this paper the Fourier transform works as one of the most important tools for calculations. We adopt the following unitary convention of the Fourier transform and Sobolev norms.

For a function f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, Fourier transform ℱ⁡[f]\mathcal{F}[f] is defined as below and equivalently denoted by f^\hat{f}.

(2.2) ℱ⁡[f]​(ξ):=12​π​∫ℝf⁡(x)​e−i​ξ​x​𝑑x.\mathcal{F}[f](\xi):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)e^{-i\xi x}dx.

As a consequence, Fourier inverse transform is given as follows.

(2.3) ℱ−1​[f^]​(x):=12​π​∫ℝf^​(ξ)​ei​ξ​x​𝑑ξ.\mathcal{F}^{-1}[\hat{f}](x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\hat{f}(\xi)e^{i\xi x}d\xi.
Definition 2.

A function f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} that can be Fourier transformed is in Sobolev space HσH^{\sigma} if the following quantity is finite. Also, we use this quantity as the norm of Hσ​(ℝ)H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{R}).

(2.4) ‖f‖Hσ​(ℝ):=(∫ℝ(1+ξ2)σ​|f^​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ)12.||f||_{H^{\sigma}(\mathbb{R})}:=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+\xi^{2})^{\sigma}|\hat{f}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.

2.1. Explicit Solution of the Linearized Equation

After executing the Fourier transform w^:=ℱ⁡[w]\hat{w}:=\mathcal{F}[w], (2.1) becomes the transport equation in the frequency domain.

(2.5) w^t+(k4+k2)​w^−∂k(k3​w^)=0.\hat{w}_{t}+(k^{4}+k^{2})\hat{w}-\partial_{k}(k^{3}\hat{w})=0.

Since the first derivative in kk indicates that (2.5) is transport type, we look for the trajectory map ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) such that f​(t):=w^​(t,ϕ​(t))f(t):=\hat{w}(t,\phi(t)) satisfies:

(2.6) d​fd​t=w^t−k3​w^k.\frac{df}{dt}=\hat{w}_{t}-k^{3}\hat{w}_{k}.

This leads to the ODE for the trajectory: ϕ′​(t)=−ϕ​(t)3\phi^{\prime}(t)=-\phi(t)^{3}, which can be explicitly solved with the given initial data ϕ⁡(0)=k0\phi(0)=k_{0}.

(2.7) ϕ⁡(t)=k01+2​k02​t.\phi(t)=\frac{k_{0}}{\sqrt{1+2k_{0}^{2}t}}.

It is notable that ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) is bounded in (−1/2​t,1/2​t)(-1/\sqrt{2t},1/\sqrt{2t}), even though the initial data is distributed all over the frequency space. That is, w^​(t,⋅)\hat{w}(t,\cdot) is compactly supported for all t>0t>0 and thus w⁡(t,⋅)w(t,\cdot) is analytic according to the Paley-Wiener theorem. Along the characteristic curve (t,ϕ⁡(t))(t,\phi(t)) lying in the t−kt-k plane, the solution for (2.5) is

(2.8) w^(t,ϕ(t))=f(t)=f(0)exp(−∫0t(ϕ(s)4−2ϕ(s)2)ds).\hat{w}(t,\phi(t))=f(t)=f(0)\exp\left(-\int_{0}^{t}(\phi(s)^{4}-2\phi(s)^{2})ds\right).\\

Here f⁡(0)=w^​(0,k⁡(0))=w^0​(k0)f(0)=\hat{w}(0,k(0))=\hat{w}_{0}(k_{0}) and ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s) is given by (2.7). Also, the integrations in the exponents are calculated as follows.

(2.9) ∫0tϕ​(s)4​𝑑s=∫0tk04(1+2​k02​s)2​ds=k04​t1+2​k02​t,∫0t2​ϕ​(s)2​𝑑s=∫0t2​k021+2​k02​s​ds=log⁡(1+2​k02​t).\begin{split}\int_{0}^{t}\phi(s)^{4}ds&=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{k_{0}^{4}}{(1+2k_{0}^{2}s)^{2}}ds=\frac{k_{0}^{4}t}{1+2k_{0}^{2}t},\\ \int_{0}^{t}2\phi(s)^{2}ds&=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{2k_{0}^{2}}{1+2k_{0}^{2}s}ds=\log(1+2k_{0}^{2}t).\\ \end{split}

Now we can head to the solution of (2.1) with the inverse Fourier transform of w^​(t,k)\hat{w}(t,k). Substituting kk with ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) and fixing tt, we can express the inverse Fourier transform as an integration over k0k_{0}. It is easy to check that it actually fulfills (2.1) and the initial condition.

2.3. Properties of S⁡(t)S(t)

The operator S⁡(t)S(t) which generates the solution of (2.1) satisfies inequalities useful for the later sections. In this section we list them and verify ones not proven above. While looking into the stability of w⁡(t,x)w(t,x) we have seen L∞L^{\infty} properties.

  • •

    If u∈(L1∩H1)​(ℝ)u\in(L^{1}\cap H^{1})(\mathbb{R}), then S⁡(t)​uS(t)u is bounded in time and converges to zero, uniformly. In particular, for the asymptotic stability of w=0w=0, u∈L1u\in L^{1} is sufficient.

  • •

    If u∈L1​(ℝ)u\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}), then ∂xnS⁡(t)​u\partial_{x}^{n}S(t)u always converges to zero as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty and the higher order derivatives decay faster.

5. Well-posedness of the Perturbative Equation

In the previous sections we just assumed that the perturbation v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) exists as a solution of (1.2) and is unique with strong regularities. Now we prove the following three remaining statements. Each statement is rigorously stated in the subsection handling it.

  • •

    Existence: There is a global-in-time mild solution for (1.2).

  • •

    Uniqueness: If v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} both solve (1.2) with the same initial data, then they are identical.

  • •

    Regularity: If the initial data v0v_{0} is sufficiently small, then ‖vx​(t,⋅)‖L∞​(ℝ)||v_{x}(t,\cdot)||_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})} is bounded by the initial value itself.

Appendix A Classification of Steady Solutions of SGM

In the introduction we have mentioned that there are three types of steady solutions u~​(x)\tilde{u}(x) for (1.1). Here we describe how those solutions look like. Taking u~t=0\tilde{u}_{t}=0, every term of (1.1) is at least twice differentiated. Integrating twice yields c1​x+c2c_{1}x+c_{2} on the right hand side and we restrict ourselves to the untilted case where c1=0c_{1}=0. According to the invariance under constant shift, the ODE for the steady solution becomes

(A.1) u~x​x+u~+u~x2=0.\tilde{u}_{xx}+\tilde{u}+\tilde{u}_{x}^{2}=0.

The following theorem presents all the possible types of steady solutions satisfying (A.1), which will be proved throughout this appendix.

Theorem A.1.

Consider steady SGM equation (A.1) with u~​(0)=u~0\tilde{u}(0)=\tilde{u}_{0} and u~x​(0)=0\tilde{u}_{x}(0)=0. If u~0<1/2\tilde{u}_{0}<1/2, then the steady solution u~​(x)\tilde{u}(x) exists for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and is periodic. However, if u~0>1/2\tilde{u}_{0}>1/2, then u~​(x)\tilde{u}(x) blows up in negative direction in finite length so that the solution exists only for a certain bounded interval. Furthermore, the singularity at the end has logarithmic scale. Finally in the case of u~0=1/2\tilde{u}_{0}=1/2, it has the explicit solution u⁡(x)=(1/2)−(1/4)​x2u(x)=(1/2)-(1/4)x^{2} so that the solution exists in the whole real line but blows up at infinity.

A.1. Phase Portrait Behavior

We first analyze the phase portrait of (A.1). Letting v~​(x):=eu~​(x)\tilde{v}(x):=e^{\tilde{u}(x)} i.e. u~=log⁡v~\tilde{u}=\log\tilde{v}, it is bounded below by zero as long as the solution exists.

(A.2) v~x​x+v~​log⁡v~=0.\tilde{v}_{xx}+\tilde{v}\log\tilde{v}=0.

And this equation can be converted into a series of two first-order autonomous equations. For further discussions we would treat the independent variable xx as the time tt in dynamical systems theory.

(A.3) {p′​(t)=q⁡(t)q′​(t)=−p⁡(t)​log⁡p​(t)(p⁡(0),q⁡(0))=(p0,q0)\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}p^{\prime}(t)&=&q(t)\\ q^{\prime}(t)&=&-p(t)\log p(t)\\ (p(0),q(0))&=&(p_{0},q_{0})\end{array}\right.

Note that p≥0p\geq 0 with the convention p​log⁡p|p=0=0p\log p|_{p=0}=0. Then (p,q)=(1,0)(p,q)=(1,0) is the only fixed point of the system. Defining F⁡(p,q):=(q,−p​log⁡p)F(p,q):=(q,-p\log p), then F∈C∞​((0,∞)×ℝ)F\in C^{\infty}((0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}) and eigenvalues of ∇F​(1,0)\nabla F(1,0) are ±i\pm i. Since this system has the Hamiltonian H⁡(p,q)=14​p2​(1−2​log⁡p)−12​q2H(p,q)=\frac{1}{4}p^{2}(1-2\log p)-\frac{1}{2}q^{2} conserved throughout the trajectory, level sets near (1,0)(1,0) become closed curves. A.2. Singularity Scale of Steady Solutions

As we know the condition under which the steady solution forms singularities in finite length, now we investigate how those singularities look like. Note that the singularity near x∼Lx\sim L corresponds to p∼0p\sim 0 or t∼T∗t\sim T^{*}. In this region d​q/d​p∼0dq/dp\sim 0 along the solution.

Also from the definition p=v~=eu~p=\tilde{v}=e^{\tilde{u}} we obtain u~​(x)=log⁡p⁡(x)∼log⁡(L−x)\tilde{u}(x)=\log p(x)\sim\log(L-x). This is the same for the opposite side due to the symmetry of the equation under x→−xx\rightarrow-x. Therefore the solution exists in the bounded interval (−L,L)(-L,L) and it blows up in logarithmic scale.
